title: Random Forest
body:
Grow hundreds of [[Decision Tree|decision trees]], each on a different random slice of the
problem, and let them vote. **The instability that makes a single tree unreliable is exactly what
makes a forest work**, which is the neatest idea in this block.

## Two sources of randomness

| Randomness | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Bagging** (bootstrap aggregating): each tree trains on a random sample of the rows, drawn with replacement | trees see different data, so they make different mistakes |
| **Feature subsampling**: at each split, each tree may only consider a random subset of the columns | stops every tree from picking the same dominant feature first |

The second one is what makes it a *random forest* rather than just bagged trees, and it matters
more than it sounds. With one very predictive feature, every bagged tree splits on it at the root
and they all end up nearly identical, which defeats the point.

Then: majority vote for [[Classification]], average for regression.

## Why voting helps

Errors have to be **uncorrelated** for averaging to cancel them. If every tree is wrong in the
same way, a thousand of them are wrong in that way too. All the machinery above exists to force
disagreement.

Given disagreement, the averaging argument is [[STATISTICS]]: independent estimates of the same
quantity have their variance divided by the number averaged. A single deep tree is low-bias and
high-variance ([[Bias]]); averaging many of them keeps the low bias and kills the variance. **You
are not making the trees better, you are making their mistakes cancel.**

This is why deliberately *not* pruning the individual trees is fine here, and would be a mistake
in a single tree.

| | Single [[Decision Tree]] | Random forest |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | modest | strong, often the best off-the-shelf option on tabular data |
| Variance | high | low |
| Readable | **yes, that is the point** | no, and that is the cost |
| Tuning needed | pruning, depth | works well with defaults |

**The trade is interpretability.** One tree explains itself; five hundred trees voting explain
nothing, so the forest lands in the same box as a [[Neural Network]] for any purpose where the
reason matters. Feature-importance scores recover a little of it, not the reasoning.

The same "combine many weak models" idea covers boosting (train each model on the previous one's
mistakes) and stacking. Those are not on this course and have no note; boosting is the one worth
knowing exists, because gradient-boosted trees usually beat forests on tabular data.
